youtube.baslik: Does noise in the other ear change this ear's emissions? #shorts
youtube.aciklama: Noise presented to the opposite ear activates the medial olivocochlear reflex, which lowers the gain of the outer hair cells, the cochlear amplifier, and reduces the otoacoustic emission amplitude in the test ear. This reduction, called contralateral suppression, is usually about 1 to 2 decibels in normal adults. In auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder, suppression is usually absent even though emissions are present.

Noise in the other ear triggers the brainstem's medial olivocochlear reflex.
This reflex lowers outer hair cell gain, so emission amplitude drops.
In normal adults, this drop is usually about one to two decibels.
In auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder, suppression is usually absent despite OAEs.
